paras: The killing of James W. Edloe was the fatal shooting of a Black political officeholder by Williamsburg, Virginia, policeman A. T. Clowes on the night of October 13, 1888. Clowes claimed self-defense, a coroner's jury found that he fired the fatal shot, and he was jailed, examined, and later released on $3,000 bail. Papers noted the large Black crowds that gathered, and one dispatch said a lynching of the officer was feared.
Edloe, described as a "mulatto" of about thirty-eight and "of fair education," was a prominent Mahone politician and deputy treasurer for Williamsburg and James City county under Rev. John M. Dawson.

According to the account of the case "as given the writer" at the preliminary examination, Clowes intervened in a quarrel between Edloe and Eli Parker and threatened to arrest Edloe, who accused him of failing to arrest a Democrat and called him a liar and a "renegade." Clowes then knocked Edloe down with a stick, and Edloe left vowing to kill him before morning. In this version Edloe returned with a pistol in each hand, surrendered them to Mayor T. M. Southal, and was shot as he ascended the store platform where Clowes stood, Clowes not knowing he had been disarmed.

The shot struck Edloe above the right ear about 8 o'clock, and he died within three minutes in front of R. T. Casey's store. His body lay on the platform for about two hours while a crowd, "almost entirely colored," grew, until Rev. Dawson, pastor of the colored Baptist church, urged it to refrain from violence and the excitement subsided.

A coroner's jury of three white and three colored men found that Edloe died from a pistol fired by Clowes, and Clowes was held in the city jail. An immense number of Black mourners, many from York and James City counties, attended Edloe's funeral on October 15. Justice R. T. Casey opened the preliminary examination on October 16 before a large crowd and continued it to the next morning. On October 27 Judge Farthing admitted Clowes to $3,000 bail on habeas corpus, and no report of an indictment or trial was found.

The Richmond Dispatch carried the story from a first telegram, "Killed by a Policeman," through local correspondence and court notes over two weeks. Its Williamsburg correspondent called the shooting "universally regretted" yet predicted a finding of justifiable homicide, and its examination story set out the defense sequence of events. Beyond Richmond, the Washington Evening Post headed a Norfolk dispatch "A Policeman Shoots a Negro" and stressed that "the negroes" might try to lynch the officer, while the Alexandria Gazette gave the case one sentence.

The only detailed account of the shooting came from the examination as told to the Dispatch writer and followed Clowes's claim of self-defense, while the coroner's verdict as printed named only who fired.

reader.title: Killing of James W. Edloe
bases: A Williamsburg policeman shot and killed Edloe after a quarrel and was jailed and examined in court; no mob took part in the killing, and the only talk of lynching was a feared attempt against the officer (A1, A4, A5, A2).

The Richmond Dispatch telegram and correspondence and a separate Norfolk dispatch in the Evening Post agree that policeman Clowes shot and killed Edloe on the night of October 13 and claimed self-defense (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: Officer's claim (wire report)
accounts.gist: Clowes claimed he killed Edloe in self-defense.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Edloe came to his death from a pistol held and fired by policeman A. T. Clowes; the verdict as printed says nothing on justification.

accounts.label: Examination account 'as given the writer'
accounts.gist: After Edloe defied and insulted Clowes, Clowes knocked him down with a stick; Edloe vowed to kill him, returned with two pistols that the Mayor took, and was shot mounting the platform by Clowes, who had not learned he was disarmed.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch reported the inquest and examination in detail under 'The Williamsburg Homicide', but its correspondent called the shooting 'universally regretted' and predicted it would be found justifiable homicide, and its examination story gave the defense-favorable sequence.
The Evening Post ran a Norfolk dispatch, 'A Policeman Shoots a Negro', centering fears that 'the negroes' might lynch the officer; the Alexandria Gazette ran one sentence.

conflicts.note: Almost certainly the same Williamsburg policeman; the local correspondence and court notes use A. T. Clowes.
